note: Luke's long “travel narrative” begins with a solemn line: Jesus {lk 9:51 τὸ πρόσωπον ἐστήρισεν τοῦ πορεύεσθαι εἰς Ἰερουσαλήμ} (“set his face to go to Jerusalem”). Rebuffed by a Samaritan village, James and John ask {lk 9:54 θέλεις εἴπωμεν πῦρ καταβῆναι ἀπὸ τοῦ οὐρανοῦ} (“do you want us to call down fire from heaven?”), as Elijah did in 2 Kings 1. Many later manuscripts add “as Elijah did” and a longer rebuke. Jesus refuses.

Only Luke has a second, larger mission. Manuscripts disagree over whether the number is seventy or seventy-two, perhaps reflecting the number of nations in Genesis 10, which also varies between the Hebrew and the Greek. On their return Jesus says {lk 10:18 Ἐθεώρουν τὸν Σατανᾶν ὡς ἀστραπὴν ἐκ τοῦ οὐρανοῦ πεσόντα} (“I watched Satan fall like lightning from heaven”), but tells them to rejoice instead that {lk 10:20 τὰ ὀνόματα ὑμῶν ἐγγέγραπται ἐν τοῖς οὐρανοῖς} (“your names are written in heaven”).

Only Mark quotes the opening of the Shema, {mk 12:29 Ἄκουε Ἰσραήλ} (“Hear, O Israel”), and his scribe is friendly: Jesus tells him {mk 12:34 Οὐ μακρὰν εἶ ἀπὸ τῆς βασιλείας τοῦ θεοῦ} (“you are not far from the kingdom”). Matthew and Luke both make the questioner a {mt 22:35 νομικὸς πειράζων αὐτόν} (“lawyer, testing him”), a minor agreement. Matthew adds {mt 22:40 ἐν ταύταις ταῖς δυσὶν ἐντολαῖς ὅλος ὁ νόμος κρέμαται} (“on these two commandments **hangs** the whole Law”).

The lawyer asks {lk 10:29 τίς ἐστίν μου πλησίον} (“who is my neighbor?”), a question about whom to love. Jesus answers with a different question: {lk 10:36 τίς τούτων τῶν τριῶν πλησίον δοκεῖ σοι γεγονέναι} (“which of these three **became** a neighbor?”). The hero is a member of a despised group, and the Samaritan {lk 10:33 ἐσπλαγχνίσθη} (“was moved with compassion”), the same verb Luke uses of Jesus at Nain and of the prodigal's father. Only Luke tells this parable.

Mary sits at Jesus' feet, the position of a student (Paul is educated “at the feet of Gamaliel”, Acts 22:3), a role normally reserved for men. The doubled name {lk 10:41 Μάρθα Μάρθα} is affectionate, as in “Simon, Simon”. Manuscripts vary on the next words; SBLGNT reads {lk 10:42 ὀλίγων δέ ἐστιν χρεία ἢ ἑνός} (“few things are needed, or only one”). John knows the same sisters with the same traits: Martha serves (John 12:2).

Matthew's denunciation is a whole chapter (23); Luke sets his shorter version at a Pharisee's dinner table. With 48 minor agreements, it is another Mark–Q overlap. Matthew's {mt 23:24 διϋλίζοντες τὸν κώνωπα τὴν δὲ κάμηλον καταπίνοντες} (“straining out a gnat and swallowing a camel”) may preserve an Aramaic pun (*qalmā* / *gamlā*). The tithed herbs differ: Luke has {lk 11:42 τὸ ἡδύοσμον καὶ τὸ πήγανον} (“mint and **rue**”), Matthew mint, dill and cumin.

Only Luke tells this parable, introduced by a warning against {lk 12:15 πάσης πλεονεξίας} (“all kinds of greed”). God's verdict is blunt: {lk 12:20 Ἄφρων ταύτῃ τῇ νυκτὶ τὴν ψυχήν σου ἀπαιτοῦσιν ἀπὸ σοῦ} (“Fool! This night your life is **demanded back** from you”). *Apaiteō* is a commercial verb for calling in a loan: the man's life was itself on loan. A shorter version also appears in the Gospel of Thomas (saying 63).

With 91 minor agreements, this is the densest overlap of Mark and Q on the site. The thief saying is almost identical, except that Matthew says {mt 24:43 ποίᾳ φυλακῇ} (“in which **watch** of the night”) where Luke says {lk 12:39 ποίᾳ ὥρᾳ} (“at what **hour**”). Luke's opening, {lk 12:35 Ἔστωσαν ὑμῶν αἱ ὀσφύες περιεζωσμέναι} (“let your waists be belted”), echoes the Passover instruction of Exodus 12:11. Only Luke grades the punishment by how much each servant knew.

Luke alone mentions two disasters of the day that are otherwise unknown to history: Galileans {lk 13:1 ὧν τὸ αἷμα Πιλᾶτος ἔμιξεν μετὰ τῶν θυσιῶν αὐτῶν} (“whose blood Pilate mixed with their sacrifices”) and the eighteen killed when {lk 13:4 ὁ πύργος ἐν τῷ Σιλωὰμ} (“the tower in Siloam”) fell. Jesus refuses to read them as punishment. The barren fig tree then gets {lk 13:8 καὶ τοῦτο τὸ ἔτος} (“one more year”). Luke has no fig-tree cursing.

Only Luke has this sabbath healing. Jesus calls the woman {lk 13:16 θυγατέρα Ἀβραὰμ} (“a daughter of Abraham”), a phrase found nowhere else in the New Testament. The argument is a wordplay on “untie”: you untie your ox on the sabbath to water it, so {lk 13:16 οὐκ ἔδει λυθῆναι} (“was it not necessary that she be **untied**?”) from her bondage of eighteen years. Again Luke uses *dei*, the word of divine necessity.

The words are almost identical, but the placement changes the meaning. Luke has Jesus say it on the road, before he reaches Jerusalem, so {lk 13:35 οὐ μὴ ἴδητέ με ἕως ἥξει ὅτε εἴπητε Εὐλογημένος ὁ ἐρχόμενος} (“you will not see me until you say ‘Blessed is he who comes’”) is fulfilled at the Palm Sunday entry. Matthew places it **after** the entry ({mt 23:39 ἀπ ἄρτι}, “from now on”), so it points to the second coming. Luke also has Jesus call Herod {lk 13:32 τῇ ἀλώπεκι ταύτῃ} (“that fox”).

Another sabbath healing found only in Luke, at a Pharisee's dinner. The argument resembles Matthew's sheep-in-a-pit saying (12:11), but in Luke the case is {lk 14:5 υἱὸς ἢ βοῦς εἰς φρέαρ} (“a **son** or an ox fallen into a well”). Some manuscripts read “a donkey or an ox”, likely a scribe's attempt to make the pairing more natural. Dropsy (fluid retention) was a stock image for insatiable greed among ancient moralists, which may explain why this healing introduces sayings about banquets.

Two pieces of table advice found only in Luke, both ending in reversal. The first ends with the maxim {lk 14:11 πᾶς ὁ ὑψῶν ἑαυτὸν ταπεινωθήσεται} (“everyone who exalts himself will be humbled”), which Luke repeats at 18:14. The second tells the host to invite {lk 14:13 πτωχούς ἀναπείρους χωλούς τυφλούς} (“the poor, crippled, lame, blind”). The same four groups are brought in a few verses later in the parable of the great banquet.

Probably the same parable, told two very different ways. Luke's host is a householder whose guests make excuses, such as {lk 14:20 Γυναῖκα ἔγημα} (“I just got married”, a valid exemption from war in Deuteronomy 24:5). Matthew's is a {mt 22:2 βασιλεῖ} (“king”) holding his son's wedding, whose troops {mt 22:7 τὴν πόλιν αὐτῶν ἐνέπρησεν} (“burned their city”). Many read that as an allusion to Jerusalem in 70 CE, and so date Matthew after it. Others see a prophecy, or a stock image of a king's punishment, and many traditional readers think Jesus told two different parables. Luke's {lk 14:23 ἀνάγκασον} (“compel them”) was later used by Augustine to justify coercing heretics.

Luke pairs the shepherd with a woman who searches for {lk 15:8 δραχμὰς ἔχουσα δέκα} (one of “ten drachmas”, each about a day's wage). Then the parable of the two sons. The father, seeing the son far off, {lk 15:20 ἐσπλαγχνίσθη καὶ δραμὼν} (“was moved with compassion and **ran**”), undignified behavior for a patriarch. The refrain {lk 15:24 νεκρὸς ἦν καὶ ἀνέζησεν ἦν ἀπολωλὼς καὶ εὑρέθη} (“was dead and is alive, was lost and is found”) ties the three parables together.

Perhaps the most puzzling parable in the Gospels, found only in Luke. A manager about to be fired cuts his master's debtors' bills, and {lk 16:8 ἐπῄνεσεν ὁ κύριος τὸν οἰκονόμον τῆς ἀδικίας} (“the master praised the dishonest manager”). *Ho kyrios* may be the master in the story or Jesus himself (“the Lord”), and the Greek doesn't settle it. The moral, {lk 16:9 ποιήσατε φίλους ἐκ τοῦ μαμωνᾶ τῆς ἀδικίας} (“make friends with unrighteous mammon”), has puzzled readers ever since.

A short bridge passage, found only in Luke. The Pharisees, {lk 16:14 φιλάργυροι ὑπάρχοντες} (“being lovers of money”), {lk 16:14 ἐξεμυκτήριζον αὐτόν} (“turned up their noses at him”): the verb comes from *myktēr*, “nostril”. Many historians think Luke's portrait of Pharisees as money-lovers is a polemical generalization, since Josephus describes them as living simply. Read more narrowly, it describes the particular Pharisees listening that day. The next parable, the rich man and Lazarus, answers them.

The only figure invented for a parable of Jesus who is given a name (Abraham, who also appears, is a figure from scripture): {lk 16:20 πτωχὸς δέ τις ὀνόματι Λάζαρος} (“a poor man named Lazarus”, Hebrew *Eleazar*, “God helps”). The rich man is unnamed; “Dives” is just Latin for “rich”. The ending is pointed: {lk 16:31 οὐδ ἐάν τις ἐκ νεκρῶν ἀναστῇ πεισθήσονται} (“they won't be convinced even if someone rises from the dead”). In John, a man named Lazarus **does** come back from the dead, and the authorities respond by plotting.

Luke's mustard-seed faith uproots a tree ({lk 17:6 τῇ συκαμίνῳ ταύτῃ}, “this mulberry tree”) and plants it in the sea, where Matthew and Mark have faith that moves a mountain. Then a stark parable about duty, found only in Luke, ending {lk 17:10 Δοῦλοι ἀχρεῖοί ἐσμεν} (“we are unworthy slaves; we have only done what we ought”). *Achreioi* literally means “useless” or “owed nothing”, that is, no special credit for doing one's job.

Only Luke tells this healing. Of ten lepers healed, one returns to give thanks, {lk 17:16 καὶ αὐτὸς ἦν Σαμαρίτης} (“and he was a **Samaritan**”). Jesus calls him {lk 17:18 ὁ ἀλλογενὴς οὗτος} (“this foreigner”). *Allogenēs* appears nowhere else in the New Testament, but it is the word carved on the Jerusalem temple's warning inscriptions, which forbade any foreigner, on pain of death, to pass into the inner courts.

Only Luke tells this parable. The judge gives in to a persistent widow, he admits, {lk 18:5 ἵνα μὴ εἰς τέλος ἐρχομένη ὑπωπιάζῃ με} (“so she won't finally wear me out”). *Hypōpiazō* is a boxing term, literally “give a black eye”, which makes this one of the few comic lines in the Gospels. The argument runs from lesser to greater: if even he yields, will not God {lk 18:7 ποιήσῃ τὴν ἐκδίκησιν τῶν ἐκλεκτῶν αὐτοῦ} (“vindicate his chosen ones”)?

The Pharisee prays {lk 18:11 πρὸς ἑαυτὸν} (“to/about himself”), ambiguous in Greek. The tax collector prays {lk 18:13 Ὁ θεός ἱλάσθητί μοι τῷ ἁμαρτωλῷ} (“God, be merciful to me, **the** sinner”). The verb is the language of atonement sacrifice, and the article makes him *the* sinner par excellence. He went home {lk 18:14 δεδικαιωμένος} (“justified”), one of the few places a Gospel uses Paul's key word in Paul's sense.

Mark's Jesus adds {mk 10:12 καὶ ἐὰν αὐτὴ ἀπολύσασα τὸν ἄνδρα αὐτῆς} (“and if **she** divorces her husband…”), which reflects Roman law, where a wife could initiate divorce, more than Jewish practice. Yet the saying had a target close at hand: Herodias, a Jewish princess, had left her husband to marry Herod Antipas. Matthew drops that line and inserts his exception, {mt 19:9 μὴ ἐπὶ πορνείᾳ} (“except for sexual immorality”), as he did in the Sermon. He alone adds the enigmatic saying about those who become {mt 19:12 εὐνοῦχοι} (“eunuchs”) for the kingdom's sake.

Mark says that when the disciples turned the children away, Jesus {mk 10:14 ἠγανάκτησεν} (“was **indignant**”). Matthew and Luke both omit his anger, part of the pattern of softening Jesus' emotions. Luke makes the children {lk 18:15 τὰ βρέφη} (“babies”). Matthew omits Mark's saying about receiving the kingdom {mk 10:15 ὡς παιδίον} (“like a child”) here, because he used it already at 18:3. Mark and Luke share 29 words in a row.

A famous theological edit. In Mark the man calls Jesus “good teacher” and Jesus objects: {mk 10:18 Τί με λέγεις ἀγαθόν οὐδεὶς ἀγαθὸς εἰ μὴ εἷς ὁ θεός} (“why do you call **me** good? No one is good but God alone”). Matthew rewrites both question and answer: {mt 19:17 Τί με ἐρωτᾷς περὶ τοῦ ἀγαθοῦ} (“why do you ask me about **what is good**?”). Only Mark says Jesus, looking at him, {mk 10:21 ἠγάπησεν αὐτὸν} (“loved him”). He is “young” only in Matthew and a “ruler” only in Luke.

Only Matthew tells this parable: everyone receives a full day's wage, from the dawn workers to those hired an hour before sunset. The owner's question is literally {mt 20:15 ἢ ὁ ὀφθαλμός σου πονηρός ἐστιν ὅτι ἐγὼ ἀγαθός εἰμι} (“or is your eye **evil** because I am **good**?”). The “evil eye” is the Jewish idiom for envy and stinginess (see the sound-eye saying in 6:23). It ends {mt 20:16 οἱ ἔσχατοι πρῶτοι} (“the last will be first”).

The most detailed of the three predictions, almost a summary of the Passion narrative. Mark's scene is eerie: Jesus walks ahead {mk 10:32 καὶ ἐθαμβοῦντο οἱ δὲ ἀκολουθοῦντες ἐφοβοῦντο} (“and they were amazed, and those who followed were afraid”). Mark says they will {mk 10:34 ἀποκτενοῦσιν} (“kill”) him. Matthew is the first to make the method explicit, {mt 20:19 σταυρῶσαι} (“crucify”). Luke stresses incomprehension: {lk 18:34 ἦν τὸ ῥῆμα τοῦτο κεκρυμμένον ἀπ αὐτῶν} (“this saying was hidden from them”).

In Mark, James and John ask for the best seats themselves. Matthew has {mt 20:20 ἡ μήτηρ τῶν υἱῶν Ζεβεδαίου} (“the mother of the sons of Zebedee”) ask, taking some of the embarrassment off the apostles. Mark's climax is one of the few places Jesus explains his death: {mk 10:45 δοῦναι τὴν ψυχὴν αὐτοῦ λύτρον ἀντὶ πολλῶν} (“to give his life as a **ransom** for many”). Luke moves the dispute to the Last Supper and drops the ransom: {lk 22:27 ἐγὼ δὲ ἐν μέσῳ ὑμῶν εἰμι ὡς ὁ διακονῶν} (“I am among you as one who serves”).

Mark names the beggar, {mk 10:46 ὁ υἱὸς Τιμαίου Βαρτιμαῖος} (“the son of Timaeus, Bartimaeus”), translating the Aramaic *bar* (“son of”) in advance. He is the only person Jesus heals in Mark who is named. Matthew doubles him, {mt 20:30 δύο τυφλοὶ} (“two blind men”), as with the Gerasene. Only Mark has the vivid gesture {mk 10:50 ἀποβαλὼν τὸ ἱμάτιον αὐτοῦ} (“throwing off his cloak”). Luke has the healing happen as Jesus **approaches** Jericho, where Mark has him leaving it. A traditional solution: there were two Jerichos, the old town and Herod's new one, a short walk apart.

Only Luke tells this story. Jesus says {lk 19:5 σήμερον γὰρ ἐν τῷ οἴκῳ σου δεῖ με μεῖναι} (“**today** I **must** stay at your house”), using two of Luke's favorite words. Zacchaeus promises to repay {lk 19:8 τετραπλοῦν} (“fourfold”), the penalty in Exodus 22:1 for a stolen sheep, well beyond what the Law required for fraud. The closing line, {lk 19:10 ζητῆσαι καὶ σῶσαι τὸ ἀπολωλός} (“to seek and save the lost”), echoes God as shepherd in Ezekiel 34:16.

Same skeleton, different numbers. Matthew's master gives {mt 25:15 πέντε τάλαντα} (“five talents”), two, and one, each about twenty years' wages. Luke's nobleman gives {lk 19:13 δέκα μνᾶς} (“ten minas”) to ten servants, one each, a mina being 1/60 of a talent. Luke weaves in a second plot: citizens who send a delegation saying {lk 19:14 Οὐ θέλομεν τοῦτον βασιλεῦσαι ἐφ ἡμᾶς} (“we don't want this man to rule over us”). This closely matches what happened when Herod's son Archelaus went to Rome in 4 BCE.
